% ================================================================
% An introduction to surds.
%
% A first sheet on surds for a lower ability Year 10 class, designed
% to be worked through with the calculator on the desk. Surds are
% met first as square roots whose decimals never end. Pupils then
% work out a mixed list of surds and multiples of surds on the
% calculator and spot which of them are equal, which leads into the
% rule for simplifying surds. Adding and subtracting surds is built
% on collecting like terms in algebra, and multiplying and dividing
% surds is taught straight from the formulas, with the formulas for
% each part boxed. The sheet ends with "many ways to make a surd"
% diagrams: one worked example, then diagrams with less and less
% filled in. Answers are on the last page.
%
% The sheet is written on, so every question is followed by a
% working area. The \newpage commands in the body are placed so that
% no question is split across the fold.
% ================================================================

\pagestyle{empty}
\linespread{1.15}\selectfont
\setlength{\parskip}{5pt}
\setlist[enumerate,1]{label=\textbf{Q\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*, itemsep=10pt, topsep=6pt, parsep=4pt}
\setlist[enumerate,2]{label=(\alph*), leftmargin=*, itemsep=8pt, topsep=5pt, parsep=3pt}
\setlength{\multicolsep}{4pt}
\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}

\newcommand{\ansline}[1][2.2cm]{\underline{\hspace{#1}}}
% A short gap for a single number, sized to sit inside a line of maths.
\newcommand{\gap}{\underline{\hspace{0.7cm}}}
% A gap under a root sign. An underline leaves too little room beneath the
% radical, so a faint dotted box marks where the number is written instead.
% The box is the tallest that still keeps the ordinary-sized root sign,
% and is measured in em so that it scales with the type around it.
\newcommand{\rootgap}{\tikz[baseline=0pt]\draw[gray!60,densely dotted,thick]
  (0,-0.12em) rectangle (1.8em,0.83em);}

\tikzset{fnkey/.style={draw=black!75,fill=black!75,text=white,rounded corners=2.5pt,
    font=\small\bfseries,minimum height=6mm,minimum width=9mm,inner sep=2pt},
  nmkey/.style={fnkey,draw=black!45,fill=black!8,text=black}}
\newcommand{\calckey}[1]{\tikz[baseline=(k.base)]\node[fnkey] (k) {#1};}
\newcommand{\numkey}[1]{\tikz[baseline=(k.base)]\node[nmkey] (k) {#1};}
\newcommand{\sqrtkey}{\calckey{$\sqrt{\blacksquare}$}}
\newcommand{\sdkey}{\calckey{S$\Leftrightarrow$D}}
\newcommand{\calcscreen}[2]{%
  \tikz[baseline=(s.center)]{%
    \node[draw=black!60,fill=teal!6!gray!12,rounded corners=2pt,
      minimum width=3.7cm,minimum height=1.3cm] (s) {};
    \node[anchor=north west,font=\small] at ([xshift=3pt,yshift=-2pt]s.north west) {#1};
    \node[anchor=south east,font=\small] at ([xshift=-4pt,yshift=3pt]s.south east) {#2};}}

% ----------------------------------------------------------------
% A "many ways to make" diagram: a surd in the middle, joined to five
% boxes that each hold a calculation whose answer is that surd.
% \spider{<middle>}{<addition>}{<subtraction>}{<multiplication>}
%        {<division>}{<single square root>}
% Any box, or the middle, can be left empty for pupils to fill in.
\newcommand{\spiderbox}[4]{%
  \node[draw=blue!45!black,rounded corners=3pt,thick,fill=white,
    minimum width=3.0cm,minimum height=1.15cm] (#1) at (#2) {};
  \node[font=\scriptsize\itshape,text=gray!70!black,anchor=north,inner sep=2pt]
    at (#1.north) {#3};
  \node[font=\small] at ([yshift=-0.12cm]#1.center) {#4};
  \draw[gray,thick] (m) -- (#1);}
\newcommand{\spider}[6]{%
  \begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current bounding box.north)]
    \node[draw=green!35!black,fill=green!8,circle,thick,minimum size=1.3cm,
      inner sep=1pt,font=\large] (m) at (0,0) {#1};
    \spiderbox{sa}{0,2.2}{an addition}{#2}
    \spiderbox{ss}{2.45,0.55}{a subtraction}{#3}
    \spiderbox{sm}{1.65,-1.85}{a multiplication}{#4}
    \spiderbox{sd}{-1.65,-1.85}{a division}{#5}
    \spiderbox{sr}{-2.45,0.55}{a single square root}{#6}
  \end{tikzpicture}}

\begin{document}

\begin{ealglossed}
\begin{center}
  {\Large\bfseries An Introduction to \ealgloss{Surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne}}\\[6pt]
\end{center}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{keyidea}
\begin{ealglossed}
A \textbf{\ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny}} is a \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} that cannot be written exactly as a \ealgloss{whole number}{liczba całkowita nieujemna} or a \ealgloss{fraction}{ułamek}, such as $\sqrt{2}$. 
\end{ealglossed}
\end{keyidea}

\begin{ealglossed}
\parttitle{1}{\ealgloss{Square roots}{Pierwiastki} on the calculator}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
The \textbf{\ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek}} of a number is the number that gives it when it is
multiplied by itself. For example $\sqrt{9}=3$, because $3\times3=9$.
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
To find a \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} on the calculator we press the \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} button, type
the number and press equals. Many calculators give the answer as a \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny}. To
see the answer as a \ealgloss{decimal}{ułamek dziesiętny}, press the S$\Leftrightarrow$D button.
\end{ealglossed}

\vspace{4pt}
\begin{center}
\sqrtkey\;\numkey{7}\;\calckey{$=$}
\quad$\longrightarrow$\quad
\calcscreen{$\sqrt{7}$}{$\sqrt{7}$}
\quad$\longrightarrow$\quad
\sdkey
\quad$\longrightarrow$\quad
\calcscreen{$\sqrt{7}$}{$2.645751311$}
\end{center}
\vspace{2pt}

\begin{ealglossed}
The calculator shows $\sqrt{7}=2.645751311$, but the \ealgloss{decimal}{ułamek dziesiętny} does not stop at
the edge of the screen. It carries on forever, so we write $\sqrt{7}$ instead.
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{enumerate}

\item \begin{ealglossed}
Use the \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} button to complete the table. When the answer is not
a \ealgloss{whole number}{liczba całkowita nieujemna}, \ealgloss{truncate}{obcinaj} to the first four \ealgloss{decimal places}{miejsca dziesiętne}.

\vspace{2pt}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.9}
\begin{tabular}{|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{2.6cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{5.2cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{3.4cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{\ealgloss{Square root}{Pierwiastek}} & \textbf{Calculator answer} & \textbf{Is it a \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny}?}\\
\hline
$\sqrt{16}$ & $4$ & No\\ \hline
$\sqrt{2}$ & & \\ \hline
$\sqrt{49}$ & & \\ \hline
$\sqrt{3}$ & & \\ \hline
$\sqrt{10}$ & & \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{ealglossed}

\end{enumerate}

\newpage

\begin{ealglossed}
\parttitle{2}{\ealgloss{Surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne} that are equal}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
 $3\sqrt{2}$ means
$3\times\sqrt{2}$, which is three lots of $\sqrt{2}$, in the same way that
$3x$ means $3\times x$ in \ealgloss{algebra}{algebra}. To find $3\sqrt{2}$ we press
\numkey{3}\;\sqrtkey\;\numkey{2}\;\calckey{$=$} on the calculator.
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \begin{ealglossed}
Use your calculator to find each answer, \ealgloss{truncated}{obcięte} to four \ealgloss{decimal places}{miejsca dziesiętne}.
\end{ealglossed}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.},itemsep=14pt]
  \item $2\sqrt{2}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{12}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{6}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{18}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{20}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $2\sqrt{3}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{8}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $3\sqrt{5}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $2\sqrt{5}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $3\sqrt{2}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
\end{enumerate}
\end{multicols}

  \item \begin{ealglossed}
Four pairs of numbers in part (a) are equal to each other. Write down
        the four pairs, in \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny} form. Two of the numbers do not have a partner.
\end{ealglossed}

\vspace{8pt}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]

\vspace{14pt}
\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]

\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]

\vspace{14pt}
\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]
\end{multicols}
\end{enumerate}

\end{enumerate}

\begin{ealglossed}
The pairs in Q2 are equal because we can \ealgloss{factor}{dzielnik} out a \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa}. For example $8=4\times2$, and $\sqrt{4}=2$, so
$\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$. Writing $\sqrt{8}$ as $2\sqrt{2}$
is called \textbf{\ealgloss{simplifying}{uproszczenie}} the \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny}.
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
\begin{formulas}{\ealgloss{simplifying}{uproszczenie} \ealgloss{surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne}}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.9}%
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\large}p{5.2cm}@{\hspace{1em}}l@{}}
$\sqrt{a\times b}=\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}$
  & for example \; $\sqrt{20}=\sqrt{4\times5}=\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{5}=2\sqrt{5}$\\
\end{tabular}

\vspace{4pt}
In words: split the number under the \ealgloss{root}{pierwiastek} into a \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa} multiplied by
another number. The \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} of the \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa} is written in front of
the \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny}.

\vspace{4pt}
\ealgloss{Square numbers}{Liczby kwadratowe}: \; $4$, \; $9$, \; $16$, \; $25$, \; $36$, \; $49$, \; $64$,
\; $81$, \; $100$
\end{formulas}
\end{ealglossed}

\newpage

\begin{ealglossed}
\begin{wex}{\ealgloss{simplify}{uprość} $\sqrt{18}$}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.2em}}l@{}}
\textbf{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa}.}
  & $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9\times2}$\\[8pt]
\textbf{Step 2 --- split the \ealgloss{root}{pierwiastek}.} & $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}$\\[8pt]
\textbf{Step 3 --- take the \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} of the \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa}.}
  & $\sqrt{18}=3\times\sqrt{2}=3\sqrt{2}$\\
\end{tabular}
\end{wex}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item \begin{ealglossed}
Fill in the gaps in parts (a) and (b), then \ealgloss{simplify}{uprość} parts (c) to (h) in
the same way.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \ealgloss{Simplify}{Uprość} $\sqrt{12}$.

\vspace{2pt}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.2em}}l@{}}
\textbf{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa}.}
  & $\sqrt{12}=\sqrt{\rootgap\times3}$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 2 --- split the \ealgloss{root}{pierwiastek}.} & $\sqrt{12}=\sqrt{\rootgap}\times\sqrt{3}$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 3 --- take the \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} of the \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa}.}
  & $\sqrt{12}=\gap\times\sqrt{3}=\gap\sqrt{3}$\\
\end{tabular}}

  \item \ealgloss{Simplify}{Uprość} $\sqrt{50}$.

\vspace{2pt}
{\small
\begin{tabular}[b]{@{}l@{\hspace{1.2em}}l@{}}
\textbf{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa}.}
  & $\sqrt{50}=\sqrt{\rootgap\times\rootgap}$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 2 --- split the \ealgloss{root}{pierwiastek}.} & $\sqrt{50}=\ansline[3.5cm]$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 3 --- take the \ealgloss{square root}{pierwiastek} of the \ealgloss{square number}{liczba kwadratowa}.}
  & $\sqrt{50}=\ansline[3.5cm]$\\
\end{tabular}}
\end{enumerate}
\end{ealglossed}
\begin{multicols}{3}
\begin{enumerate}[resume]
  \item $\sqrt{24}$
  \item $\sqrt{28}$
  \item $\sqrt{45}$
  \item $\sqrt{63}$
  \item $\sqrt{75}$
  \item $\sqrt{98}$
\end{enumerate}
\end{multicols}

\end{enumerate}

\newpage

\begin{ealglossed}
\parttitle{3}{Adding and subtracting \ealgloss{surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne}}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item \begin{ealglossed}
\textbf{Warm-up.} \ealgloss{Simplify}{Uprość} each \ealgloss{expression}{wyrażenie} by collecting \ealgloss{like terms}{wyrazy podobne}. If
an \ealgloss{expression}{wyrażenie} cannot be \ealgloss{simplified}{uproszczone}, write it as it is.
\end{ealglossed}
\begin{multicols}{3}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $2x+4x=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $5y-2y=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $a+3a=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $6m-m=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $4x+2y+x=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $x+y=\ansline[1.6cm]$
\end{enumerate}
\end{multicols}

\end{enumerate}

\begin{ealglossed}
\ealgloss{Like terms}{Wyrazy podobne} have the same letter, and we collect them by adding or subtracting
the numbers in front. \ealgloss{Surds}{Pierwiastki niewymierne} are collected in the same way: a \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny} such as
$\sqrt{3}$ is collected just like the letter $x$. \ealgloss{Surds}{Pierwiastki niewymierne} with the same number
under the \ealgloss{root}{pierwiastek}, such as $2\sqrt{3}$ and $4\sqrt{3}$, are called \textbf{\ealgloss{like surds}{pierwiastki podobne}}. A \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny} with no number in front has $1$ lot, so $\sqrt{3}=1\sqrt{3}$,
just as $x=1x$.
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
\begin{formulas}{adding and subtracting \ealgloss{like surds}{pierwiastki podobne}}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.9}%
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\large}p{6.6cm}@{\hspace{1em}}l@{}}
$a\sqrt{n}+b\sqrt{n}=(a+b)\sqrt{n}$ & for example \; $2\sqrt{3}+5\sqrt{3}=7\sqrt{3}$\\
$a\sqrt{n}-b\sqrt{n}=(a-b)\sqrt{n}$ & for example \; $9\sqrt{2}-4\sqrt{2}=5\sqrt{2}$\\
\end{tabular}

\vspace{4pt}
In words: add or subtract the numbers in front, and keep the \ealgloss{surd}{pierwiastek niewymierny} the same.
\end{formulas}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{warning}
\begin{ealglossed}
Only \ealgloss{like surds}{pierwiastki podobne} can be collected. Just as $x+y$ cannot be \ealgloss{simplified}{uproszczone},
$\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}$ cannot be \ealgloss{simplified}{uproszczone}. It is \textbf{not} $\sqrt{5}$: on
the calculator $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}=3.146264\ldots$, but
$\sqrt{5}=2.236067\ldots$
\end{ealglossed}
\end{warning}

\begin{ealglossed}
\begin{wex}{collecting \ealgloss{like surds}{pierwiastki podobne}}
\small
Each line of \ealgloss{surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne} is collected in the same way as the \ealgloss{algebra}{algebra} beside it.

\smallskip
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{3em}}l@{}}
\textbf{\ealgloss{Algebra}{Algebra}} & \textbf{\ealgloss{Surds}{Pierwiastki niewymierne}}\\
$2x+4x=(2+4)x=6x$ & $2\sqrt{3}+4\sqrt{3}=(2+4)\sqrt{3}=6\sqrt{3}$\\
$7y-3y=(7-3)y=4y$ & $7\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2}=(7-3)\sqrt{2}=4\sqrt{2}$\\
$4x+2y+x=5x+2y$ & $4\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}=5\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{3}$\\
\end{tabular}
\end{wex}
\end{ealglossed}

\newpage

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item \begin{ealglossed}
Fill in the gaps in parts (a) and (b), then \ealgloss{simplify}{uprość} parts (c) to (j)

\item \begin{ealglossed}
The \textbf{\ealgloss{perimeter}{obwód}} of a shape is the total length of its sides.
\end{ealglossed}

\newpage

\begin{ealglossed}
\parttitle{4}{Multiplying and dividing \ealgloss{surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne}}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
Part 2 showed that $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}$. Read the other way
round, this says $\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{18}$: when we multiply two
\ealgloss{square roots}{pierwiastki}, we multiply the numbers under the \ealgloss{roots}{pierwiastki}. Dividing works in the
same way. Remember that $ab$ means $a\times b$.
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
\begin{formulas}{multiplying and dividing \ealgloss{surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne}}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.95}%
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\large}p{8.4cm}@{\hspace{1em}}l@{}}
$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{ab}$ & for example \; $\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{6}$\\
$\sqrt{a}\div\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{a\div b}$ \; or \; $\dfrac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{b}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{a}{b}}$
  & for example \; $\sqrt{15}\div\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{5}$\\
$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{a}=a$ & for example \; $\sqrt{7}\times\sqrt{7}=7$\\
$m\sqrt{a}\times n\sqrt{b}=mn\sqrt{ab}$ & for example \; $2\sqrt{3}\times4\sqrt{5}=8\sqrt{15}$\\
$m\sqrt{a}\div n\sqrt{b}=(m\div n)\sqrt{a\div b}$ & for example \; $8\sqrt{6}\div2\sqrt{3}=4\sqrt{2}$\\
\end{tabular}

\vspace{4pt}
In words: multiply or divide the numbers under the \ealgloss{roots}{pierwiastki}. Numbers in front are
multiplied or divided separately.
\end{formulas}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{ealglossed}
\begin{wex}{multiplying \ealgloss{surds}{pierwiastki niewymierne}}
\small
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{2em}}l@{}}
$\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{5}=\sqrt{3\times5}=\sqrt{15}$ & \\
$\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{2\times8}=\sqrt{16}=4$
  & the answer can be a \ealgloss{whole number}{liczba całkowita nieujemna}\\
$2\sqrt{3}\times4\sqrt{5}=(2\times4)\sqrt{3\times5}=8\sqrt{15}$
  & the numbers in front are multiplied separately\\
\end{tabular}
\end{wex}
\end{ealglossed}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item \begin{ealglossed}
Fill in the gaps in parts (a) and (b), then work out parts (c) to (j)
using the \ealgloss{formulas}{wzory}. Some of the answers are \ealgloss{whole numbers}{liczby całkowite nieujemne}.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{7}=\sqrt{\rootgap\times\rootgap}=\sqrt{\rootgap}$
  \item $3\sqrt{2}\times5\sqrt{7}=(\gap\times\gap)\sqrt{\rootgap\times\rootgap}
        =\ansline[1.6cm]$
\end{enumerate}
\end{ealglossed}

  & the numbers in front are divided separately\\
\end{tabular}
\end{wex}
\end{ealglossed}
